text: Before any file reaches a table, it lands somewhere Snowflake can see it first. That landing zone is called a stage, and every load — whether you run it by hand or automate it — passes through one.
Creating a named external stage is mostly point and click. Pick your cloud provider — here it's Amazon S3 — and Snowsight writes the exact same CREATE STAGE statement you could have typed yourself.
A stage is really just a pointer. Running LIST at-stage proves it: these are the real files sitting in the real bucket, not a promise that something is out there.
Once you create it, the stage isn't a keyword you have to remember — it's a real object. It shows up in the object browser right alongside your tables, under Stages.

Every stage is one of two kinds. An internal stage is Snowflake-managed storage — scoped to a user, a table, or given its own name. An external stage instead points at storage you already own, in S3, Azure Blob, or GCS.
The syntax mirrors that split. An internal stage just needs a name and a file format. An external stage adds a URL and credentials, so Snowflake knows where to reach and how to authenticate.
Next: file formats. A stage tells Snowflake where a file lives — the file format tells it exactly how that file is shaped.
